title: Global Request Director: capacity‑informed affinity and progressive shed plan
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: We need a single, testable admission/routing component (Global Request Director, GRD) that makes per-request decisions across regions based on latency SLOs, real-time capacity signals, and customer affinity. Current routing is either region-first or naive latency-based — both lead to expensive cross-region tail latency and cascading overloads during regional incidents.

Goal: Deliver a production-ready GRD that: enforces SLO-aligned latency budgets, uses capacity telemetry to avoid oversubscribing a region, preserves geo-affinity when possible, and supports progressive degradation (graceful shedding) and model-tier fallbacks when resources are constrained. The system should also expose clear metrics and allow policy overrides (per-customer or per-route).
acceptance_criteria: GRD makes deterministic routing decisions for 100% of API requests when enabled; documented decision trace available in logs and console
Under normal load, >= 99.5% of requests meet configured p95 latency SLOs for their route (measured over rolling 1h windows)
When a region's capacity crosses circuit threshold, GRD opens the region-level circuit within 60s and routes 90% of new requests to fallback targets or neighboring regions according to policy

Progressive-shed rules run without request duplication: requests are either routed to lower-cost model variants, trimmed (shorter max tokens), or rejected with a clear error that contains a recommended retry strategy
Feature flags exist for: a) enabling GRD globally, b) per-route overrides, c) emergency global shedding mode
End-to-end tests and chaos experiments demonstrate no single-region incident causes >2x error budget burn for cross-region routes within a 30m incident window
technical_approach:
We will implement GRD as a stateless admission controller that queries a small set of realtime signals and consults a policy engine. Core signals: regional_capacity (active_batches, queued_tokens, free_slots), recent_tail_latency (p95/p99), and customer_affinity_score (configured per-customer). Policy evaluation is deterministic: 1) Quick pre-check for hard blocks (region disabled, customer blocklist). 2) Compute per-target score = base_latency_estimate + capacity_penalty + affinity_bonus - cost_penalty. 3) If top score target violates the route SLO budget or region-level circuit is open, consult fallback_actions: route-to-neighbor, downgrade-model-variant, reduce-max-tokens, or reject with Retry-After.

Circuit breaker choreography: region circuits evaluate a combined signal of (GPU_util >= 85% for >60s) OR (queued_tokens_per_gpu > threshold) OR (p99 request latency > p99_slo * 1.5). When open, region is deprioritized and moved to passive failover for at least a 5m cool-down. Rolling close uses gradual probe traffic.

Policy store: policies live in a central config service (versioned), with per-route and per-customer overrides. GRD caches configs for 30s and revalidates asynchronously. All decisions emit a decision_trace id for observability.
rollout_plan:
Phase 1 (canary): Implement GRD behind feature flag; route 1% of traffic for non-critical routes to GRD in us-west to validate scoring and logging. Duration 2 weeks.

Phase 2 (regional testing): Expand to 10% traffic and enable capacity-based circuits in us-west & eu-central. Run chaos tests (pod/zone failures) during a maintenance window. Duration 2 weeks.

Phase 3 (global): Enable GRD for all read-only / non-sensitive routes with model-downgrade actions allowed. Monitor errors and SLOs for 1 week, then enable for write/latency-critical routes with per-customer opt-out for enterprise customers.

Fallback: Emergency kill-switch at load-balancer to bypass GRD and restore previous routing within 1 minute.
testing_plan:
Unit tests for scoring and policy evaluation; integration tests that simulate capacity signals and verify routing outputs. Create synthetic load tests where: 1) one region is saturated and assert that GRD routes >=80% of new traffic to alternatives; 2) gradual overload causes model-downgrade path; 3) emergency open circuit routes progressively without oscillation.

Chaos suite: simulate network partitions and delayed telemetry. Observe decision_trace logs and ensure no request loops. Add automated PR checks that run a small GRD policy simulator with seeded seeds.

Run a tabletop incident drill with SRE and Product to validate messaging and rollback procedures.
dependencies: Infra-telemetry: expose region_queued_tokens and free_slots metrics
notes: Design trade-offs considered: embedding more state in GRD (per-customer counters) vs keeping it stateless for scale — chose stateless with short cache to simplify failover.
We intentionally prefer graceful degradation (downgrade model -> trim tokens -> reject) rather than immediate cross-region reroute when cost_delta > 2x to avoid bill shocks for customers.
SLO alignment: per-route SLOs are primary driver; if routing to meet SLO requires model downgrade, we will prefer it over long cross-region hops for latency-sensitive endpoints.
Open question: whether to expose an admin-level budget for emergency cross-region routing that prioritizes SLAs over unit cost. Action: follow-up decision in next review.
